title: Llama.cpp v1.0 on an RTX 3090: up to 55% faster with speculative decoding
content:
llama.cpp reached version 1.0 on 13 November 2026. This test compared it with a pre-v1 build from five days earlier (build 12199) on an RTX 3090.
- What changed: old functions and flags are removed, and there are new models, an FP8 option for the context cache, a safer llama-server on a network and a redesigned chat page.
- What 1.0 promises: from now on, a change that could break programs built on llama.cpp's code comes with a new first number, such as 2.0.
- One request at a time: the same speed as pre-v1, without speculative decoding.
- Four requests at once: 14 to 22% more text per second.
- Speculative decoding: the 27B model wrote 52 to 55% faster.
The short answer
Speeds are in tokens per second (tok/s), and higher is faster. A token is a short piece of text, often a word or part of one. Speculative decoding and MTP are explained in their own section.
Verdict: if you have an NVIDIA RTX 30-series or newer card, update if several people or programs use your server at once, or if you use speculative decoding with a larger model. If you are the only user and chat without speculative decoding, v1.0 is no faster, so update when it suits you. Either way, remove --defrag-thold from your command first.
What is llama.cpp?
llama.cpp is a free, open-source program that runs large language models on your own computer. It reads models stored as GGUF files. A GGUF file holds all of a model's weights in one file. llama.cpp runs these models on a CPU or on a GPU from NVIDIA, AMD, Intel or Apple. It is written in C and C++.
Most people use one of its programs:
- llama-server loads a model and answers requests over HTTP. It uses the same API as OpenAI, so chat apps, coding tools and agents that work with OpenAI can use it instead. It also serves a chat page in the browser.
- llama-cli lets you chat with a model in the terminal.
Many other tools run llama.cpp underneath. Ollama starts llama.cpp's llama-server for every GGUF model it loads, and LM Studio does the same on Linux. So a change in llama.cpp reaches those tools too, once they move to a newer build.
What is ggml?
ggml is the library that does the maths inside llama.cpp: it multiplies the large tables of numbers that make up a model, on whichever CPU or GPU you have. The v1.0 announcement describes ggml as a "tensor library for machine learning" and llama.cpp as "LLM inference in C/C++". Both are made by the same team, ggml-org. Most changes to ggml are first made in the llama.cpp repository and copied to ggml afterwards, as ggml's contributing guide asks. ggml also reached v1.0.0 on 13 November.
What does llama.cpp 1.0 mean?
llama.cpp has two kinds of version number, and v1.0 did not replace either of them.
- Build numbers, such as b12199, count the changes made to the code so far. A new build is published several times a day, and that has not stopped.
- Version numbers, such as v0.9.0 and v1.0.0, give some builds a release name. They started with v0.1.2 on 18 August 2026 and reached v0.9.0 on 4 November. v1.0.0 is build 12359.
The version numbers follow semantic versioning: the first number goes up only for a change that can break software built on top of llama.cpp. The announcement puts it this way: "Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps." Its table of rules says a "breaking change to the public C API" raises the first number, the major version. A new feature, a backend update or support for a new model raises the second number, the minor version. A bug fix raises the third, the patch number.
For people who run a model at home, the version rules change little. They matter to developers whose programs build on llama.cpp's code.
What changed in v1.0 for a home server
The v1.0.0 release notes list every change since v0.9.0. The ones that matter most for a home server are:
- Faster with a few tokens at a time on NVIDIA: a new CUDA kernel handles 2 to 24 tokens at once on RTX 30-series and newer cards. A kernel is a small program that runs on the GPU. The test below measures what it changes.
- Removed flag: --defrag-thold (-dt) is gone, along with older functions in the programming interface. Remove the flag from your start command before you update.
- Tools need an API key on the network: if llama-server listens on an address other than localhost and has no API key, it now refuses to turn on its built-in tools or MCP servers unless you add --allow-unauthenticated-tools. MCP servers are connections that let the model call outside programs. In this test, v1.0 in Docker would not start with --tools all and no key. It stopped with the error "server tools, MCP servers or MCP proxy are enabled on a non-loopback address without an API key". Build 12199 started with the same command, and v1.0 started once --api-key was added.
- No private addresses in requests: image and media links that point to a local or private address, such as a NAS on your network, are refused unless you add --media-allow-private-urls. The chat page's MCP proxy can no longer reach local addresses at all.
- New features: an FP8 option for the context cache (-ctk f8_e4m3), a cache in system RAM for mixture-of-experts models, a text-to-speech endpoint at /v1/audio/speech, a redesigned chat page and support for new models, all listed in the release notes.
How the benchmark was run
Both builds ran on the same machine, with the same model files and the same prompts. The test scripts and raw results are on GitHub. Facts about llama.cpp on this page link to the page they come from, and figures without a link were measured in this test.
- Machine: Fedora 44, Docker 29.9.2, an NVIDIA RTX 3090 with 24 GB (driver 615.78.08), an AMD Ryzen 9 5900X with 12 cores, and 62 GB of RAM.
- Pre-v1: the official ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-cuda image from 8 November, which reports 0.9.0-dev (build 12199, commit 372dc5ca1). It is the build used in Ollama vs llama.cpp.
- v1.0: the image ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-cuda-v1.0.0-b12359-b1b770d, which reports 1.0.0-dev (build 12359, commit b1b770d90).
- Models: Qwen3.5-9B-Q4_K_M.gguf (5.7 GB) and Qwen3.5-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf (16.7 GB) from the unsloth repositories on Hugging Face. Both builds used the same files. Q4_K_M is a quantization: the model's numbers are stored in about 4 bits each, so the file is smaller and fits on the GPU. The speculative decoding test used the MTP versions of the same models, described in that section.
- Requests: a short prompt of about 70 tokens with 512 tokens generated, and a long prompt of about 4,120 tokens with 256 tokens generated. Thinking, the model's hidden reasoning step, was off. The temperature was 0, so the model always picked its most likely next token.
- Order and heat: the two builds took turns. Before each run, the script waited until the GPU had cooled to 50 °C, because a hot card slows down. Each figure is the median of five runs, unless the section says otherwise.
Tokens per second is how fast the model writes its answer, and higher is better. The context, mentioned below, is how many tokens the model can keep in view at once: the prompt, the conversation so far and the answer.
Speed with one request: the same as before
This is the common case at home: one person chats with the model, and the server works on one request at a time, without speculative decoding.
The two builds were within 2% of each other. v1.0 was slightly ahead with the 9B model and slightly behind with the 27B model. But the five runs of one build varied by more than that: v1.0's short-prompt runs on the 9B model ranged from 111.8 to 118.7 tokens per second. So the test found no real difference. An earlier run on the same day, with a slightly newer v1 build, gave the same result: every speed within about 1% of pre-v1.
Both builds were a few percent slower than in the Ollama vs llama.cpp test six days earlier, where the same pre-v1 build wrote 121.6 tokens per second with the 9B model. Pre-v1 was slower by the same amount, so

report.summary: Benchmarks on an RTX 3090 show llama.cpp v1.0 delivers no single-user speedup but 14–22% more throughput with four concurrent requests and 52–55% faster speculative decoding.
report.background: llama.cpp is a free, open-source C/C++ inference engine that runs GGUF-format large language models on CPUs and on NVIDIA, AMD, Intel and Apple GPUs. Its ggml tensor library does the underlying maths, and both projects share the ggml-org team. After years of fast-moving builds, the project began issuing named releases in August 2026, reaching v0.9.0 on 4 November and v1.0.0 (build 12359) on 13 November 2026, alongside ggml v1.0.0. Crucially, llama.cpp sits underneath many popular tools: Ollama and LM Studio launch its llama-server for every GGUF model they load, so changes here ripple through the local-AI ecosystem. Version 1.0 signals a new stability promise: semantic versioning, where the first number only rises for changes that can break software built on top of the project.
key_points: Single request unchanged: with one person chatting and no speculative decoding, v1.0 and the pre-v1 build (b12199) landed within about 2% of each other, and run-to-run variance was larger than the difference. The test found no real single-user speedup, so solo users can update whenever convenient.

Concurrency gains: when the server handled four requests at once, v1.0 produced 14 to 22% more text per second. A new CUDA kernel designed for batches of 2 to 24 tokens on RTX 30-series and newer cards drives this, making v1.0 worthwhile for shared home servers used by several people or programs.

Speculative decoding boost: with the same 27B Qwen3.5 model using MTP-based speculative decoding, v1.0 wrote 52 to 55% faster. That makes the update compelling for anyone running larger models with a draft-model or MTP setup, where the small extra proposal step clearly pays off.

Breaking changes to handle: the --defrag-thold (-dt) flag is removed, so strip it from start commands before upgrading. llama-server now refuses to enable built-in tools or MCP servers on a non-loopback address without an API key, unless --allow-unauthenticated-tools is passed, and media links to private addresses are blocked by default.

Semantic versioning begins: build numbers (b12359) still tick several times a day, but version numbers now follow semver — a major bump means a breaking change to the public C API or ABI, minor bumps add features or backends, patches fix bugs. The v1.0 notes also add an FP8 context-cache option, an MoE RAM cache, a text-to-speech endpoint and a redesigned chat page.
report.impact: For the AI industry, v1.0 marks llama.cpp's transition from a fast-moving hacker project into a stable platform with a compatibility contract, which matters for downstream products like Ollama and LM Studio that embed it. Developers gain a predictable upgrade path but must adapt to stricter security defaults — API keys for network-exposed tools, blocked private URLs — and removed legacy flags, so CI scripts and Docker commands need auditing before bumping builds. Regular users see little change in day-to-day solo chatting, but anyone sharing a home server, running agents, or pairing a small draft model with a larger one gets meaningful throughput improvements without new hardware. The broader signal is that local inference keeps closing the gap with hosted APIs on cost efficiency, especially in multi-user and speculative-decoding scenarios.
report.tools: To follow up, grab the official ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-cuda image and run llama-server or llama-cli directly; the Qwen3.5 GGUF files (including MTP variants) come from unsloth on Hugging Face. Ollama and LM Studio are the easiest wrappers if you prefer not to manage flags yourself, and the test scripts and raw results are published on GitHub so you can reproduce the benchmark on your own card.
